title: PadRemote wire protocol v1
description: One WebSocket carries two logical streams. Text frames are JSON control/event messages defined by `controlMessage` below. Binary frames are batched touch samples defined by `binaryTouchFrame` (documented here; JSON Schema cannot describe a binary layout, so that subschema is descriptive only). The phone sends RAW TOUCHES ONLY - all gesture interpretation happens on the desktop.

challenge.title: challenge (desktop -> phone, first message on every connection)
challenge.description: The desktop speaks first, on every path (`/`, `/observe`, `/config`), and reads nothing until it has been answered. A fresh nonce per connection, so an `auth` captured off the still-unencrypted link cannot be replayed into the next one. A client that does not answer within 10 seconds - or whose first message is anything other than `auth` - is sent `error: badAuth` and closed, without ever occupying a device slot.

auth.title: auth (phone -> desktop, in reply to challenge)
auth.description: Proves the client holds a key without sending it. MUST be the first message the client sends; anything else is a failed handshake. WHICH key is decided by `device`, and that is what makes revoking one phone possible. The enrolment secret P is 128 bits, generated by the desktop, and reaches the phone only in the fragment of the QR's URL (`#k=`) - never in a query string, where a page server would log it. A phone discards P once enrolled and keeps only its device key, so a device that is forgotten cannot enrol itself again.

device.description: This device's id, chosen by the client and public. If the desktop already has it on its paired list, `hmac` MUST be signed with that device's key, K = HMAC-SHA256(P, "padremote:device:" + device) truncated to 16 bytes. If the desktop does NOT have it, this is enrolment: `hmac` MUST be signed with P itself, and the id joins the list. Enrolment deliberately does not accept a device key - a revoked phone still holds one, and accepting it would undo the revocation. Omit the field entirely to authenticate with P and NOT enrol, which is what the replay tool and the desktop's own settings and diagnostics pages do.

hmac.description: HMAC-SHA256(key, nonce) over the nonce as the ASCII text the challenge carried, lowercase hex

welcome.title: welcome (phone -> desktop, at connect)
welcome.description: Declares the surface geometry so the desktop can convert normalized coordinates into physical pixel deltas, and names the device. Several devices may be connected at once, each with its own recognizer on the desktop, so the geometry is per connection - not global.

name.description: What this device calls itself, e.g. "iPhone" or "Samsung tablet". Shown to the OTHER connected devices when they are waiting their turn with the cursor, so "another device is in control" can name it. Optional; the desktop falls back to the peer's IP address. May be re-sent at any time to rename the device.

state.title: state (desktop -> phone)
state.description: Recognizer state, for the phone's status UI.

name.description: computer name, sent once at connect

pressMs.description: How long a still finger must rest before a drag begins. Sent once at connect. The phone's long-press ring is drawn from it, so the ring finishes exactly when the drag really starts.

tapMaxPx.description: How far a finger may stray from where it landed and still count as resting. Sent once at connect. Past this the engine has committed to a cursor move and will not press the button however long the finger then rests, so the phone's ring must stop charging here and not restart until the finger lifts.

control.title: control (desktop -> phone)
control.description: Who is driving the shared cursor, and whether the computer can move it at all. Sent on connect and whenever either changes. Several devices may be connected at once, but the computer has one cursor, so exactly one of them drives it at a time: the cursor goes to whoever starts a gesture, and changes hands only at the start of a gesture, once the previous holder has been idle for a short grace period (long enough to protect the gap inside a double-tap). A device that is not driving is still read - its touches are recognised and reported - but nothing it does is injected. A page that receives active=false MUST keep its connection open and keep sending touches: taking over is done by touching the pad, not by reconnecting.

active.description: true when THIS connection is the one driving the cursor

holder.description: name of the device driving instead, when that is somebody else

devices.description: how many devices are connected in total, this one included

blocked.description: Present only when the computer will move nothing for ANYBODY, and says why: `permission` - macOS has not granted Accessibility, so it accepts every event the app posts and discards them all; `dryRun` - the app was started with --dry-run and injects nothing on purpose. The phone MUST show this rather than a healthy link, and MUST keep sending touches: `permission` is cleared without a reconnect the moment the box is ticked, and the desktop says so with a fresh `control`. This field exists because the failure is otherwise invisible from the phone - the socket is up, the gesture readout follows every finger, the latency figure is live, and the cursor sits perfectly still.

settings.title: settings (phone -> desktop)
settings.description: An OVERRIDE of what the computer says. The desktop mirrors the host's own trackpad settings, so a phone that has no opinion about a setting MUST NOT send it - sending the settings sheet's stored defaults on connect silently defeats the mirroring, and a Mac with natural scrolling off then scrolls the wrong way. Applied on top of config.json without persisting, and only to the device that sent it: a tablet and a phone are different sizes, so they keep separate sensitivities. An override survives a config or host reload; `follow` gives it back.

follow.description: Settings handed back to the computer, by name. A separate field because absence and 'match my computer again' are different requests: a phone that is simply not overriding a setting omits it, and one that is giving an override up has to say so.

effectiveSettings.title: settings (desktop -> phone)
effectiveSettings.description: What this device is actually being driven with. Sent on connect and whenever the computer's trackpad settings or config file change. The phone fills its settings sheet in from this - it has no other way to know how the user's trackpad is set, and assuming is what defeated the mirroring.

following.description: True where the value is the computer's own rather than this phone's override.

code.description: badAuth: the `auth` reply was missing, malformed or wrong - including a device key the desktop has revoked ("Forget", on the desktop's connect page); the connection is closed, and a page that retries will fail identically until it is paired again. A client that receives this SHOULD discard its stored device key, so the next scan enrols cleanly rather than adding a second id beside a dead one. unpaired: the desktop has revoked every pairing while this session was live (the user chose "Forget all devices"); the page MUST stop reconnecting and tell its user to scan the new QR. replaced: a newer connection from the SAME device - another tab, or another browser on that phone - has taken this session's place, or the user hung up on it from the desktop. The page MUST stop reconnecting: two pages racing to replace each other is the control tug-of-war that `superseded` used to cause. Unlike `superseded` this is not an eviction by a different device; a phone and a tablet stay connected and take turns (see `control`). busy: too many devices are already connected (the desktop caps concurrent devices); the connection is closed and the page should not retry on its own. superseded: LEGACY. Desktops before multi-device support drove one cursor through one shared recognizer and evicted the older connection; a page that receives it MUST stop reconnecting and wait for its user, because an automatic retry would evict the phone that just took over and the two would then trade control indefinitely. Current desktops never send it - several devices stay connected and take turns instead (see `control`).

echo.title: echo (desktop -> phone)
echo.description: Latency probe. Carries back the t_ms of the most recently processed touch sample so the page can display touch-to-cursor latency (acceptance criterion: < 50 ms on the LAN).

tMs.description: performance.now() timestamp copied from the sample that produced the most recent input action

binaryTouchFrame.title: Binary touch frame (phone -> desktop)
binaryTouchFrame.description: Little-endian. One frame batches every coalesced sample captured since the previous animation frame. Header is 2 bytes, each sample is 14 bytes, so frame length MUST equal 2 + 14*count.

const.name: count
const.description: number of samples in this frame, 1..=255

const.name: t_ms
const.description: performance.now() at the sample, truncated to ms
